name: Dynamic member lookup
first: A way for code to read a member of a type by a name that the type does not declare, which swiftc turns into a call of one subscript of the type with the name as a string.

dependsOn.why: A dynamic member subscript takes a parameter, runs its body, and returns a value, as a function does.

sil.shows: Line 9 makes the name volume into a string, which the program keeps as text.
Reading settings.volume calls the subscript of Settings.

what.is: Dynamic member lookup lets code read a member of a type by a name that the type does not declare. swiftc turns each such name into a call of one subscript of the type, with the name as a string, and the subscript works out the value.
what.afterExample: `Settings` declares no property named `volume`, yet line 9 reads `settings.volume` and prints {{7}}. The subscript on line 4 looks up `"volume"` in `values`.
what.problem: Some values have members whose names are known only when the program runs, such as the keys of a dictionary read from a file. Without dynamic member lookup, code reads them with a string in square brackets. With it, code reads them with a dot and a name, as it reads a property.
what.how: When swiftc finds a name after a dot that the type does not declare, it builds a call of the type's subscript whose argument label is `dynamicMember`, and passes the name as a string. So line 9 runs the subscript with `key` set to `"volume"`.

when.text: Use it when a type's members come from data, such as a dictionary, and code should read them with a dot and a name.
Don't use it when the names are known as you write the code. A property for each name lets swiftc check the name. With dynamic member lookup, a misspelled name still builds:

parts.name: The attribute `@dynamicMemberLookup`
parts.text: An attribute starts with an at sign, and gives swiftc more information about the declaration after it. On line 1, the attribute `@dynamicMemberLookup` lets code write member names after a dot that `Settings` does not declare. swiftc then checks that `Settings` has a subscript whose argument label is `dynamicMember`: without one, line 1 does not build.

parts.name: The dynamic member subscript, lines 4 to 6
parts.text: Lines 4 to 6 are the subscript that a type with dynamic member lookup must have. A subscript is code that runs when a value is read with square brackets, as `values[key]` is on line 5. This one's argument label is `dynamicMember`, and its parameter, `key`, gets each member name as a `String`. Its return type, `Int`, is the type of every dynamic member. Line 5 returns the value for `key` in `values`, and `??` gives 0 when `values` has no value for `key`.

parts.name: The dynamic members, lines 9 to 11
parts.text: On lines 9 to 11, the names `volume`, `brightness`, and `contrast` are written after a dot, as properties are, but `Settings` declares none of them. Each one is a dynamic member. When swiftc builds the program, it turns `settings.volume` into a call of the subscript, with `"volume"` as its argument. A name that is not a key in `values`, such as `contrast`, still builds.

steps.text: Line 8 makes a `Settings`, and stores it in `settings`. Its `values` holds 7 for `"volume"` and 4 for `"brightness"`.
Line 9 reads `settings.volume`. `Settings` declares no member named `volume`, so this is a call of the subscript on line 4, with `key` set to `"volume"`.
Line 5 returns the value for `"volume"` in `values`, which is 7.
Line 10 reads `settings.brightness`, so the subscript runs again, with `key` set to `"brightness"`. Line 5 returns 4, and line 10 prints {{4}}.
Line 11 reads `settings.contrast`, and the subscript runs with `key` set to the string "contrast". `values` has no value for it, so `??` on line 5 gives 0, and line 11 prints {{0}}.

end.text: `Settings` declares no `volume`. swiftc turns `settings.volume` into a call of the dynamic member subscript with `"volume"`, and the subscript returns the value.
